nature-eco-729.q: Where does methanogenesis sit in the breakdown of biomass in oxygen-free environments?
nature-eco-729.a: It is the final stage of anaerobic digestion, the last step in decomposing biomass where there is no oxygen.

nature-eco-448.q: What does the Ramsar Convention do for wetlands?
nature-eco-448.a: It lists wetlands of international importance and promotes their wise use; it has worked since 1971.

nature-eco-734.q: Why do methanotrophs matter for global warming?
nature-eco-734.a: They reduce the amount of methane emitted to the atmosphere in the global methane budget.

nature-eco-416.a: All the plants, animals and microbes of a woodland working together with their non-living physical surroundings.

nature-eco-743.q: What kind of plants drive shrub encroachment on rangelands?
nature-eco-743.a: Native plants, not alien invasives; they can shift open grasslands and savannas to closed woodlands.

nature-eco-445.q: What can constructed wetlands remove from wastewater?
nature-eco-445.a: Using plants, soil and organisms, they remove suspended solids, organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus and pathogens.

nature-eco-411.a: Root-like tubes that stick up out of the mud like straws so the plant can breathe.

nature-eco-418.q: How does clearing forest into smaller patches reduce biodiversity?
nature-eco-418.a: It makes it harder for forest species to find food, shelter and mates.

nature-eco-720.q: Which water-cycle quantities can remote sensing measure?
nature-eco-720.a: Surface water storage, soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration, and snow and ice.

nature-eco-456.q: How many people benefit from coral reef ecosystem services?

nature-eco-482.q: What do riparian zones do for the waters beside them?
nature-eco-482.a: They act as natural biofilters, shielding waters from too much sediment, polluted runoff and erosion.

nature-eco-507.q: What three kinds of stress can affect freshwater ecosystems?
nature-eco-507.a: Physical (temperature, flow, light), chemical (nutrients, oxygen-consuming materials, toxins) and biological (over-harvesting, exotic species).

nature-eco-548.q: What are large marine ecosystems and how many are there?
nature-eco-548.a: A concept developed by the US agency NOAA in 1984 to guide conservation; there are 66, contributing an estimated $3 trillion a year and 90% of the world's annual marine fish catch.

nature-eco-463.q: How does a meandering river build a floodplain?
nature-eco-463.a: It erodes the outside of each bend and deposits a point bar on the inside, building a level floodplain.

nature-eco-432.q: Why do extra nutrients change which plants win in a salt marsh?
nature-eco-432.a: Salt marsh plants are normally limited by nitrogen, so extra nutrients reshuffle which species win the competition.

nature-eco-436.q: How much of the breakdown of organic matter in oxygen-poor sediment can sulfate-reducing bacteria account for?

nature-eco-704.q: What is Antarctica's make-up as the world's largest cold desert?
nature-eco-704.a: About 98% ice sheet and 2% barren rock.

nature-eco-476.q: How much peat must land have to be called a peatland?
nature-eco-476.a: At least 30 cm, even if it has been drained.

nature-eco-509.a: Floating mats of moss and sedge, about half a meter thick, that move when walked on.

nature-eco-493.q: What do most seagrass restoration projects plant?
nature-eco-493.a: Cuttings, rhizome fragments or cores taken from donor meadows; few projects use seeds.

nature-eco-566.q: How big are permafrost emissions per degree of warming, according to the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report?
nature-eco-566.a: It estimates 14-175 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent per 1 C of warming.

nature-eco-549.q: Why are tidal flats important to migratory shorebirds?
nature-eco-549.a: They are key stopovers that let tens of millions of migratory shorebirds travel between breeding and non-breeding areas.

nature-eco-547.q: What do mangroves and seagrasses do for coral reefs?
nature-eco-547.a: They regulate the sediment, freshwater and nutrients that reach coral reefs.

nature-eco-736.q: At what depths do oxygen minimum zones typically lie?
nature-eco-736.a: About 200 to 1,000 meters; their upper edge is a sharp oxygen gradient called the oxycline.

nature-eco-695.q: Why are benthic macroinvertebrates good water-quality indicators?
nature-eco-695.a: They are almost always present, easy to sample and identify, visible to the naked eye, short-lived and generally sedentary.

nature-eco-723.q: What is allochthony in an aquatic food web?
nature-eco-723.a: The share of aquatic food web biomass derived from allochthonous material.

nature-eco-495.q: How do archaea produce methane in wetland soils?
nature-eco-495.a: By fermenting acetate, or by combining hydrogen with carbon dioxide.

nature-eco-541.q: What are the three layers of a stratified lake?
nature-eco-541.a: The warm upper epilimnion, the cold bottom hypolimnion, and the thermocline, the band of rapid temperature change between them.

nature-eco-518.q: Why are hydrothermal vent ecosystems unusual?
nature-eco-518.a: They are among the few ecosystems on the planet that do not depend on sunlight for energy.

nature-eco-440.q: What do green and blue infrastructure include in cities?
nature-eco-440.a: Green infrastructure includes nature preserves and added vegetation such as vertical gardens; blue infrastructure includes stormwater management such as bioswales.

nature-es-001.q: What term did the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment popularize?
nature-es-001.a: Ecosystem services, meaning the benefits people gain from ecosystems.

nature-es-011.q: What do life-cycle assessment impact methods link to ecosystem services?
nature-es-011.a: They link pressures such as land-use change and eutrophication to changes in ecological functions and ecosystem services.

nature-es-010.q: What features mark ecosystem service decisions in land planning?
nature-es-010.a: They are usually spatial, always have several objectives, and rest on uncertain data, models and estimates.

nature-es-108.q: How did the 1996 World Food Summit define food security?
nature-es-108.a: All people at all times having physical and economic access to enough safe, nutritious food for an active, healthy life.

nature-es-103.q: How did New York City purify its water as an ecosystem service?
nature-es-103.a: It restored its polluted Catskill Watershed rather than rely only on treatment when its water fell below EPA standards.

nature-es-094.q: How much do honeybees' crop pollination benefits to global food production come to?

nature-es-111.q: How much abiotic pollination is done by wind?

nature-es-115.q: Besides honey bees, what do growers use to pollinate crops?
nature-es-115.a: Blue orchard bees, bumblebees, hand pollination and even machines.

nature-val-073.q: Who first proposed contingent valuation surveys, and for what?
nature-val-073.a: S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup, in 1947, to value a non-market good.

nature-val-055.q: Who developed the idea of option value and when?
nature-val-055.a: Burton Weisbrod, in 1964, resting it on uncertain future need, irreversible or costly loss, and the asset not being storable.

nature-val-087.q: What did Robert Costanza and colleagues estimate in 1997?
nature-val-087.a: The first estimate of the worldwide worth of ecosystem services: $33 trillion a year.

nature-val-080.q: What independence assumption does the multinomial logit make about choices?
nature-val-080.a: Independence of irrelevant alternatives: the odds between two options do not depend on what other options are present.

nature-val-083.q: How does Daniel Kahneman explain insensitivity to the number of birds saved?
nature-val-083.a: As judgment by prototype: people price a mental image, such as one oil-soaked bird, rather than the number affected.

nature-val-107.q: What can regulation do to conduct?
nature-val-107.a: It may prescribe or proscribe conduct (command-and-control), calibrate incentives, or shape preferences.

nature-val-109.q: How do mild and wild risk differ?
nature-val-109.a: Mild risk obeys the law of large numbers and is relatively predictable; wild risk, with possibly infinite mean or variance, makes that law ineffective and is hard or impossible to predict.

nature-val-010.a: Energy savings: the saved energy is never consumed.

nature-val-040.a: By their results, such as whether they maximise well-being, which treats nature instrumentally.

nature-val-033.q: Why is there a tendency to overexploit and underproduce nature under commodification?
nature-val-033.a: Because nature's value cannot be fully counted in money.

nature-acct-018.q: Who coined Gross National Happiness and when?
nature-acct-018.a: Bhutan's 4th King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, in 1972, declaring it more important than GDP.

nature-acct-116.q: What question underlies the World Happiness Report rankings?
nature-acct-116.a: One life-evaluation question, the Cantril ladder, in which respondents rate their current life from 0 (worst) to 10 (best); the data come mainly from the Gallup World Poll.

nature-acct-107.a: Using up natural resources by mining, quarrying, drilling or felling.

nature-clim-264.q: What is carbon intensity per kilowatt-hour used for?
nature-clim-264.a: It is widely used to compare sources of electricity.

nature-acct-055.q: What did the 2024 Living Planet report show about monitored wildlife populations?
nature-acct-055.a: They fell by an average of 73% between 1970 and 2020.

nature-acct-037.q: Is there a universal standard for sustainable development indicators?
nature-acct-037.a: No; disciplines and international organizations have proposed many different indicators.

nature-acct-069.q: How many indicators does the 2024 Environmental Performance Index use, and for how many countries?
nature-acct-069.a: It uses 58 indicators to rank 180 countries on climate change mitigation, ecosystem vitality and environmental health.
